headline: After a warm Monday in the 60s and a cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday, a large storm late Wednesday night through Friday brings 1–2 inches of rain, east-northeast winds gusting 35–45 mph and widespread coastal flooding on Thanksgiving.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Sunday night's rain is basically over for New York City: the low is passing north and east of Montauk faster than expected, so rain chances were lowered after midnight. Any lingering light rain is limited to the North and South Forks of Long Island and New London County, Connecticut, and should end by 2 AM. No impacts are expected, and wind is no longer a concern overnight.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Monday stays dry and unusually warm, with highs in the 60s even as a cold front passes in the afternoon and brings northwest gusts around 20 mph; record highs are mostly around 70 (72 at Central Park, 74 at Newark), so new records look unlikely, though Islip has tied or broken its record high each of the last four days. Tuesday and Wednesday turn much colder and stay dry as an unusually strong area of high pressure builds from the Great Lakes into the Northeast. Highs struggle to get out of the 40s, and overnight lows drop mostly below freezing, except in the New York City metro area Wednesday morning.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A much larger storm brings potentially significant impacts from late Wednesday night into Friday, with a broad west-to-east band of rain stretching from the Ohio Valley to off the Atlantic coast, so escaping bad weather for Thanksgiving is unlikely. East-northeast winds build Wednesday into Thursday and peak during the day Thursday at 20–30 mph with gusts of 35–45 mph, possibly 50 mph at the coast, strongest in the New York City metro area and along the coast. Rain totals of 1–2 inches look reasonable, and the storm is carrying a lot of moisture thanks to a strong southern jet stream tied to El Niño. Some computer models track the low farther west along the Appalachians, but strong winds are expected either way; a chance of rain lingers mainly Friday morning, with west winds gusting around 30–35 mph.

coast: No Coastal Flood Statement is planned for Monday morning's high tide, since water levels should fall short of flooding thresholds along the back bays of Nassau County. Thursday is the big concern: with a full moon on the 24th and king tides this week, many spots need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding, and the current forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, perhaps even localized major flooding, plus beach flooding, erosion and overwash. On the water, Small Craft Advisories run until 6 PM Monday for Long Island Sound east of the Connecticut River and until 6 AM Tuesday for the nearshore ocean waters, driven by large ocean waves and lingering high seas. After a possible brief lull Tuesday afternoon and night, east-northeast winds ramp up Wednesday, reaching gale force on the ocean Wednesday night and storm force Thursday, with gales on the Sound and bays late Wednesday night into Thursday; peak waves reach 15–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on Long Island Sound and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound.
watch_for: Widespread minor to moderate, possibly localized major, coastal flooding on Thursday with king tides and the full moon.
Strong east-northeast winds Thursday, gusting 35–45 mph and possibly 50 mph at the coast.
The storm's track: a path farther west along the Appalachians would change rain and wind details.
confidence: Forecasters are confident tonight's rain is ending and that a warm Monday and cold, dry Tuesday and Wednesday follow; a significant Thanksgiving storm looks likely, but the exact extent of its rain, wind and coastal flooding impacts is still uncertain.
